segments.en: Picture a river, wide and brown and slow, with mangroves along its banks and a pirogue gliding past. Now picture a country that follows that river inland like a ribbon. That is The Gambia.

It is the smallest country on mainland Africa, a narrow strip of land on either side of the Gambia River, wrapped almost entirely by Senegal. Only at its western end does it open onto the Atlantic Ocean.
Gambians call their home the Smiling Coast, and the name suits it. A simple hello often turns into a long, friendly chat about family, health and where you've come from.

Greetings are important here and never rushed. In Wolof you might hear Nanga def? meaning how are you? and the reply, Maa ngi fi rekk, I'm right here. English is the official language, used in schools and offices.
The capital, Banjul, sits on an island where the river meets the sea. Along the coast, Serrekunda and Bakau hum with markets, music and the smell of fish grilling on the beach.

At Kachikally, in Bakau, there is a sacred pool where crocodiles lie calmly in the sun. For many families it is a place of blessing, and visitors are sometimes allowed to touch a sleepy crocodile very gently.

Head upriver and the land grows quieter. Rice fields shine green in the rainy season, chimpanzees live on protected river islands, and bird watchers come from far away to spot hundreds of colourful species.
Kunta Kinteh Island, in the middle of the river, is a place of memory. It recalls the Atlantic slave trade and the millions of people taken from West Africa, and it is visited in quiet respect.

Music is at the heart of Gambian life. Griots, the keepers of history and song, play the kora, a harp with twenty-one strings made from a large gourd. Their music tells of kings, heroes and family lines.
Wrestling is a much-loved sport, with drums, dancing and great excitement before each bout. Football is everywhere too, from dusty village pitches to the beach at sunset.

At the table, try domoda, a rich peanut stew served over rice, or benachin, a one-pot rice dish cooked with fish or meat and vegetables. Meals are often shared from one big bowl, eaten with the right hand.

Afterwards, someone may brew attaya, strong sweet green tea poured from high up to make it foamy, served in three rounds while everyone talks. Stay for all three, then cross the border into Senegal, which is waiting all around you.
